claim: Hallucinations occur in both normal and clinical populations.
source: Hallucinations occur in both normal and clinical populations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrett (1993, 1994) in the introduction section.

claim: Visual hallucinations can be induced in the normal population by visual flicker limited to an annulus.
source: Here we show that visual hallucinations can be induced in the normal population by visual flicker, limited to an annulus that constricts content complexity to simple moving grey blobs, allowing objective mechanistic investigation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from multiple experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Hallucination strength peaked at approximately 11 Hz flicker.
source: Hallucination strength peaked at ~11 Hz flicker and was dependent on cortical processing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: Hallucination strength is dependent on cortical processing.
source: Hallucination strength peaked at ~11 Hz flicker and was dependent on cortical processing.
evidence: Supported by interocular transfer experiment (Experiment 2) showing binocular neuron involvement.

claim: Hallucinated motion speed increased with flicker rate.
source: Hallucinated motion speed increased with flicker rate, when mapped onto visual cortex it was independent of eccentricity, underwent local sensory adaptation and showed the same bistable and mnemonic dynamics as sensory perception.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 3A showing speed measurements at different flicker rates.

claim: When mapped onto visual cortex, hallucinated motion was independent of eccentricity.
source: Hallucinated motion speed increased with flicker rate, when mapped onto visual cortex it was independent of eccentricity, underwent local sensory adaptation and showed the same bistable and mnemonic dynamics as sensory perception.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 3B showing consistent cortical propagation speed across eccentricities.

claim: Hallucinated motion underwent local sensory adaptation.
source: Hallucinated motion speed increased with flicker rate, when mapped onto visual cortex it was independent of eccentricity, underwent local sensory adaptation and showed the same bistable and mnemonic dynamics as sensory perception.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 8A showing increased dominance durations over time that reset with spatial location change.

claim: Hallucinations showed the same bistable and mnemonic dynamics as sensory perception.
source: Hallucinated motion speed increased with flicker rate, when mapped onto visual cortex it was independent of eccentricity, underwent local sensory adaptation and showed the same bistable and mnemonic dynamics as sensory perception.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiments 6, 9, and 10 showing bistability characteristics and memory effects.

claim: Hallucinations are generally defined as an involuntary percept-like experience in the absence of an appropriate direct stimulus.
source: Generally, hallucinations are defined as an involuntary percept-like experience in the absence of an appropriate direct stimulus (Bentall, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bentall (1990).

claim: Very little is known about the mechanisms underlying hallucinations due to methodological constraints.
source: However, very little is known about the mechanisms underlying hallucinations, due largely to the methodological constraints caused by their inherently subjective, constantly changing heterogeneous content.
evidence: Based on established understanding of the field's limitations.

claim: Visual hallucinations are thought to arise when external stimuli are overwhelmed by internally generated spontaneous patterns of neural activity.
source: Visual hallucinations are thought to arise in exceptional circumstances when external stimuli are overwhelmed by internally generated spontaneous patterns of neural activity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ffytche (2008), Butler et al. (2012), and others describing various hallucination contexts.

claim: When a white annulus was flickered on/off on a black background at approximately 2-30 Hz, light grey blobs appeared and rotated around the annulus.
source: When a white annulus was flickered on/off on a black background (~2–30 Hz), we noticed that light grey blobs appeared and rotated around the annulus, first in one direction then the other (Figure 1A; see Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by direct observation and depicted in Figure 1A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The light grey blobs remained clearly observable across the range of oscillation frequencies tested.
source: Unlike full field luminance flicker stimulation whose content changes as a function of flicker frequency (Allefeld et al., 2011; Mauro et al., 2015), the light grey blobs remained clearly observable across the range of oscillation frequencies tested.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and contrasted with cited prior work.

claim: Effective contrast of hallucinations peaked around 11 Hz and continued to decline slowly as a function of frequency.
source: Figure 1D shows the effective contrast of the hallucinations as a function of flicker frequency. Contrast estimates peaked around 11 Hz, then continued to decline slowly as a function of frequency (main effect frequency: exp. 1A F(3,81) = 3.42, p=0.021; exp. 1B: F(3,69) = 5.81, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiments 1A and 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Hallucinations in the asynchronous 2.5 Hz condition were perceived at a higher contrast than in the synchronous condition.
source: Figure 1E shows exactly this; hallucinations in the asynchronous 2.5 Hz condition were perceived at a higher contrast than in the synchronous condition (t(19) = 2.60, p=0.018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: At 21 Hz, the synchronous condition gave higher contrast values than the asynchronous condition.
source: Likewise, the same experiment performed at 21 Hz yielded the opposite pattern of results, the synchronous condition gave higher contrast values (t(19) = 2.28, p=0.034; interaction: F(1, 19) = 8.06, p=0.011), as hallucinations produced by >21 Hz flicker were perceived as lower in contrast in our first experiment (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: Flicker induced hallucinations transpire at or beyond binocular neurons and cannot be the sole product of retinal afterimages.
source: Together these data suggest that flicker induced hallucinations transpire at or beyond binocular neurons and cannot be the sole product of retinal afterimages.
evidence: Inferred from the interocular transfer experiment results showing differential effects of synchronous vs asynchronous presentation.

claim: The rotational speed of hallucinations was dependent on the annulus flicker rate, with higher frequencies giving faster rotation speeds.
source: The rotational speed was dependent on the annulus flicker rate (Figure 1F), with higher frequencies giving faster rotation speeds (F(2,10) = 24.75, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: The mean propagation speed of hallucinations over V1 surface was 5.6 cm/s.
source: Figure 1G shows longer propagation times as a function of greater neural distance, corresponding to a mean propagation speed of 5.6 cm s−1 over V1 surface.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 3B converted to cortical distance using Horton and Hoyt (1991) formulae.

claim: The percentage of time observers reported rotational motion decreased with a greater number of gaps in the flickering annulus.
source: Figure 1H shows the percentage of time observers reported rotational motion vs. stationary patterns as a function of gap number. There was a clear trend of less rotation with a greater number of gaps (F(2,6) = 14.68, p=0.005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 4A with statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage of time rotational motion was perceived decreased as a function of gap size.
source: Again, the percentage of time rotational motion was perceived went down as a function of gap size (F(2,6) = 15.93, p=0.004) (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: Unlike luminance stimuli, observers reported no pattern for over 60% of the time at isoluminance.
source: Strikingly, unlike luminance stimuli, observers reported no pattern for over 60% of the time at isoluminance (F(2,8) = 39.67, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 5 with statistical analysis.

claim: The hallucinations have a neural locus sensitive to luminance, but not color flicker, likely the dorsal visual processing stream.
source: These data suggest a neural locus sensitive to luminance, but not color flicker, likely the dorsal visual processing stream, which has a higher proportion of cells blind to isoluminance (Shapley, 1990).
evidence: Inferred from isoluminance experiment results and supported by citation to Shapley (1990).

claim: Observers hallucinated clockwise and counter-clockwise motion equal proportions of time.
source: Figure 2A shows equivalent percentages of time reported for each motion direction (CW vs CCW: t(8) < 1, p=0.53).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: The distribution of dominance durations for hallucinated bistability exhibits a long tail, forming a gamma-like distribution.
source: One classic hallmark of bistability is that the distribution of dominance durations exhibit a long tail (occasional long durations), forming a gamma-like distribution (Blake and Logothetis, 2002). Figure 2B shows a clear long tail for dominance durations for the hallucinated bistability, consistent with the core characteristic of other bistable perceptual phenomena.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 6 and comparison to established bistability characteristics.

claim: There was a significant difference between mean contrast thresholds for congruent and incongruent probe trials, with greater sensitivity when the probe was rotating congruently with the hallucinatory percept.
source: Figure 2D shows a significant difference between mean contrast thresholds for congruent and incongruent trials, with greater sensitivity to the probe stimulus when it was rotating in a congruent direction with the hallucinatory percept (t(9) = 2.8, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 7 with statistical analysis.

claim: The hallucinatory motion percept (or tracking it) weakly suppresses or boosts retina-based motion depending on the motion congruity.
source: This suggests that the hallucinatory motion percept (or tracking it) weakly suppresses or boosts retina-based motion depending on the motion congruity.
evidence: Inferred from the probe experiment results showing differential sensitivity to congruent vs incongruent motion.

claim: Dominance durations increased over time during a session of same-sized stimulus.
source: Figure 2E shows that dominance durations increased over time during a session of same-sized stimulus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 8A.

claim: In the second period of hallucination tracking, the new different-sized and non-overlapping annulus did not 'follow on' from the slower dynamics, but returned to the original shorter durations.
source: Further, in the second period of hallucination tracking, the new different-sized and non-overlapping annulus did not 'follow on' from the slower dynamics, but returned to the original shorter durations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 8A.

claim: Hallucinated bistability can undergo a form of sensory adaptation that is local in visual space.
source: These data suggest that hallucinated bistability can undergo a form of sensory adaptation that is local in visual space.
evidence: Inferred from Experiment 8A results showing reset of adaptation with spatial location change.

claim: Dominance durations increased over time, but the alternation rate was not statistically different between the three flicker rates tested.
source: Figure 2F again shows adaptation, with an increase in dominance durations over time, however across the whole period the alternation rate was not statistically different between the three flicker rates (F(2,24) = 1.76, p=0.19), suggesting the change in alternation rate was not due to flicker adaptation, but most probably due to neural fatigue in neurons representing the hallucinatory bistable structure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 8B with statistical analysis and inference about mechanism.

claim: All individual subjects showed hallucination motion stability above the chance score of 50%, with the mean significantly above chance at 75%.
source: All individual subjects show a stability measure above the chance score of 50% (two rotation directions), with the mean significantly above chance (75%; compared to 50%: p<0.001), suggesting that hallucinated bistability can be stabilized by a novel form of memory across intermittent presentations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 9 with statistical analysis.

claim: Hallucinated bistability can be stabilized by a novel form of memory across intermittent presentations.
source: All individual subjects show a stability measure above the chance score of 50% (two rotation directions), with the mean significantly above chance (75%; compared to 50%: p<0.001), suggesting that hallucinated bistability can be stabilized by a novel form of memory across intermittent presentations.
evidence: Inferred from the intermittent presentation experiment results showing above-chance stability.

claim: The rotating sphere significantly predicted hallucinated alternation rates (r = 0.312; p=0.006), while binocular rivalry did not (r = 0.133; p=0.228).
source: Figure 2H shows a scatter plot of the data, the rotating sphere (red) significantly predicted hallucinated alternation rates (r = 0.312; p=0.006), while binocular rivalry (blue) did not (r = 0.133; p=0.228).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Experiment 10 with statistical analysis.

claim: The predictive relationship between the rotating sphere and hallucinated bistability, but not rivalry, might be due to the former two both involving a common neurophysiological mechanism for motion.
source: We propose that the predictive relationship between the rotating sphere and hallucinated bistability, but not rivalry, might be due to the former two both involving a common neurophysiological mechanism for motion.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the correlation data from Experiment 10.

claim: The model is based on the idea that uniform luminance flicker stimulation resonates with the natural frequency of cortical cells to evoke standing waves of activity in primary visual cortex that induce the conscious experience of the hallucination.
source: This model is based on the idea that uniform luminance flicker stimulation resonates with the natural frequency of cortical cells to evoke standing waves of activity in primary visual cortex that induce the conscious experience of the hallucination (Billock and Tsou, 2012; Rule et al., 2011; Ermentrout and Cowan, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The standing waves/hallucinations arise when flicker frequencies are approximately twice the natural frequency of the damped oscillations in the neural dynamics.
source: The standing waves/hallucinations arise when flicker frequencies are approximately twice the natural frequency of the damped oscillations in the neural dynamics (Rule et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rule et al. (2011).

claim: The resonant frequency of simple cells in the primary visual cortex of cat typically peaks near 5 Hz.
source: The resonant frequency of simple cells in the primary visual cortex of cat typically peaks near 5 Hz (Movshon et al., 1978).
evidence: Supported by citation to Movshon et al. (1978).

claim: The natural frequency of the model was tuned to 5.5 Hz so that it elicited prominent standing waves with 11 Hz flicker to match behavioral data.
source: Here we tuned the natural frequency of the model to 5.5 Hz so that it elicited prominent standing waves with 11 Hz flicker to match our behavioral data (Figure 1D).
evidence: Describes model parameter selection based on experimental results.

claim: When stimulated with 11 Hz uniform flicker, the model generated 'cortical' standing waves at half the flicker rate.
source: When stimulated with 11 Hz uniform flicker (the stimulus parameters that gave the highest hallucinated contrast; Figures 1D and 3C), the model generated 'cortical' standing waves, that is, oscillations in modelled cortex, at half the flicker rate (Figure 3D), in accordance with previous findings.
evidence: Supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Standing waves were observed for flicker frequencies in the range 8–18 Hz, which are interpreted as hallucinatory.
source: Standing waves were observed for flicker frequencies in the range 8–18 Hz, which we interpret as hallucinatory.
evidence: Based on model simulation results and interpretation.

claim: Beyond 8-18 Hz frequencies, the cortical model produced spatially uniform responses which are interpreted as non-hallucinatory.
source: Beyond those frequencies the cortical model produced spatially uniform responses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) which we interpreted as non-hallucinatory.
evidence: Based on model simulation results and interpretation.

claim: The space-time signatures of the flicker-induced standing waves evoked identical responses from both the Left and Right motion detectors.
source: The space-time signatures of the flicker-induced standing waves evoked identical responses from both the Left and Right motion detectors (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Ambiguous motion signals induced spontaneous switching between the two perceptual populations.
source: Consequently, those ambiguous motion signals induced spontaneous switching between the two populations (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The dominance times of each perceptual decision exhibited a long-tailed distribution (M = 5.1 s, SD = 1.6 s) that was qualitatively similar to those observed experimentally.
source: The dominance times of each perceptual decision (Figure 3G) exhibited a long-tailed distribution (M = 5.1 s, SD = 1.6 s) that was qualitatively similar to those observed experimentally (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by model simulation results compared to experimental data.

claim: When the model is presented with a counter-phase retina-sourced physical patterned stimulus with identical spatial and temporal frequencies to the flicker-induced standing waves, standing waves were also produced in model-cortex.
source: When the same model is presented with a counter-phase retina-sourced physical patterned stimulus (Figure 3H), with identical spatial (fx = 0.11 cycles/mm) and temporal (ft = 5.5 Hz) frequencies to the flicker-induced standing waves (hallucinations), standing waves were also produced in model-cortex (Figure 3I; see Appendix 2).
evidence: Supported by model simulation results shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The net motion signals from counter-phase stimulation were stronger than those induced by the blank flicker stimulation.
source: The net motion signals were stronger than those induced by the blank flicker stimulation (Figure 3E and J), hence the spontaneous switching between LEFT and RIGHT perceptual decisions was somewhat faster (M = 4.3, SD = 1.5, Figure 3K and L).
evidence: Supported by model simulation results comparing Figures 3E and 3J.

claim: The data implicate retinotopically organized visual cortex as the site of bistable flicker induced hallucinations.
source: Our data implicate retinotopically organized visual cortex as the site of bistable flicker induced hallucinations.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including cortical distance mapping and interocular transfer.

claim: The technique essentially limits the hallucination space to a one dimensional annulus and one set of visual features: moving light grey blobs.
source: Unlike previous work on visual hallucinations that suffered methodological limitations due to the almost infinite array of unpredictable hallucinated features (e.g. multiple combinations of color, form and motion), our technique essentially limits the space to a one dimensional annulus and the one set of visual features: moving light grey blobs.
evidence: Describes the methodological innovation of the study.

claim: Counter-phase physical stimuli are known to induce motion percepts that spontaneously switch between the two candidate directions of motion.
source: Counter-phase physical stimuli are known to induce motion percepts that spontaneously switch between the two candidate directions of motion.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The model suggests that uniform flicker can induce spatiotemporal responses in primary visual cortex that are very similar to those induced by counter-phase physical stimuli, given the appropriate choice of spatial and temporal frequencies.
source: Our model suggests that uniform flicker can induce spatiotemporal responses in primary visual cortex that are very similar to those induced by counter-phase physical stimuli, given the appropriate choice of spatial and temporal frequencies.
evidence: Based on model simulation results comparing flicker and counter-phase stimulation.

claim: The same neural mechanism that contributes to apparent motion of a counter-phase physical stimulus also contributes to hallucinated experience.
source: We argue that the same neural mechanism that contributes to apparent motion of a counter-phase physical stimulus also contributes to hallucinated experience.
evidence: Inferred from model results showing similar cortical responses to both stimuli.

claim: Theories based on symmetry-breaking standing waves have been proposed to explain the complex spatio-dynamics of the human brain.
source: It is interesting that in general, theories based on so-called symmetry-breaking standing waves have been proposed to explain the complex spatio-dynamics of the human brain (Atasoy et al., 2016), as well as in many other physical processes such as convection in fluids, animal coat markings, and cellular division (Stewart, 1999; Turing, 1952; Kondo and Miura, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical work in neuroscience and other fields.

claim: Almost no specific treatments have been developed for clinical use for hallucinations.
source: Accordingly, almost no specific treatments have been developed for clinical use.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of clinical practice.

claim: The technique for controlling and objectively measuring hallucinated features and the corresponding neural model should prove useful in probing the mechanism(s) that allows such a range of non-ordinary function to produce hallucinations.
source: Our technique for controlling and objectively measuring the range of hallucinated features (contrast, motion, bistability) and the corresponding neural model should prove useful in probing the mechanism(s) that allows such a range of non-ordinary function to produce hallucinations.
evidence: Speculative statement about future utility of the method.

claim: 65 participants completed experiment 1, with 7 excluded from experiment 1A and 6 from experiment 1B due to poor fitting.
source: Flicker frequency (1A: 8.5 Hz, 10.6 Hz, 14.2 Hz, 21.3 Hz; 1B: 4.7 Hz, 14.2 Hz, 21.3 Hz, 30.6 Hz): 65 participants completed experiment 1 (35 in experiment 1A, 24 female; 30 in experiment 1B, 18 female). Seven were excluded from experiment 1A and six from experiment 1B due to poor fitting of a cumulative Gaussian function to their data (i.e. R2 <0.70).
evidence: Describes participant numbers and exclusion criteria.

claim: The final number of participants in Experiment 1 was 28 and 24 in experiments 1A and 1B, respectively.
source: The final number of participants was 28 (21 female) and 24 (15 female) in experiments 1A and 1B, respectively.
evidence: Describes final participant numbers after exclusions.

claim: 29 first year psychology students participated in experiment 2, with 9 excluded due to poor curve fitting, leaving 20 participants.
source: Inter-ocular transfer: 29 first year psychology students (20 female) participated in experiment 2. Nine were excluded due to poor curve fitting (see above), leaving 20 participants (14 female).
evidence: Describes participant numbers and exclusion criteria for Experiment 2.

claim: Six participants completed experiment 3A, and six completed experiment 3B.
source: Speed experiments (3A: variable flicker rate; 3B: variable eccentricity): six participants (one female) completed experiment 3A, and six (one female) completed experiment 3B. The author RC participated in both.
evidence: Describes participant numbers for Experiment 3.

claim: Four individuals participated in experiment 4A, and four participated in experiment 4B.
source: Gap experiments (4A: variable number of gaps; 4B: variable gap width): four individuals participated in experiment 4A (one female), and four participated in experiment 4B (one female), including the author RC in both.
evidence: Describes participant numbers for Experiment 4.

claim: 5 participants completed the isoluminance experiment.
source: Isoluminance experiment: 5 participants (one female) completed this experiment, including the author RC.
evidence: Describes participant numbers for Experiment 5.

claim: Nine participants completed the bistable characteristics experiment.
source: Experiment 6. Bistable characteristics experiment: nine participants (three female) completed this experiment, including the author RC.
evidence: Describes participant numbers for Experiment 6.

claim: 13 participants completed the probe experiment, with data from three participants excluded due to pre-set criteria indicating non-compliance.
source: Probe experiment: 13 participants (10 female) completed this experiment. Data from three participants were excluded due to pre-set criteria indicating non-compliance with task instructions.
evidence: Describes participant numbers and exclusion criteria for Experiment 7.

claim: Seven participants completed experiment 8A, and six completed experiment 8B.
source: Local adaptation experiments (8A: examination of local adaptation; 8B: functional impact of flicker rate): seven participants (one female) completed experiment 8A, and six (one female) completed experiment 8B, and the author RC participated in both experiments.
evidence: Describes participant numbers for Experiment 8.

claim: 8 participants completed the intermittent presentation experiment.
source: Intermitted presentation experiment: 8 participants (three female) completed this experiment, including the author RC.
evidence: Describes participant numbers for Experiment 9.

claim: 103 participants completed the individual differences alternation rate experiment, with 19 excluded due to reliability issues, leaving 84 participants.
source: Individual differences alternation rate experiment: 103 participants (67 female) completed this experiment. 19 were excluded due issues with reliability in their data (explained below). The total number of participants included in the analyses was 84 (57 female).
evidence: Describes participant numbers and exclusion criteria for Experiment 10.
